title: Loops in JavaScript
idea: A loop repeats a block of code while its test is true, or once per item. Each repeat is called a pass.

analogy.text: Laps on a track. Before each lap you check whether you have run enough; if not, you run one more.
analogy.breaks: A runner tires; a loop whose check never fails runs forever.

points: `for` and `while` test first, so the body may never run.
Use `for` when you can count the passes, `while` when you cannot.
`for...of` visits each value of an array or string, with no index to manage.
`break` leaves the loop; `continue` skips to the next pass.

steps.caption: `i` starts at 1. It counts the passes.
The test `i <= 3` is true (1 <= 3), so the body runs.
`i++` makes `i` 2. Control jumps back to the test.
Pass 2 repeats the test, the body and the update. `total` is 3, `i` is 3.
Pass 3 does the same: `total` is 6, `i` is 4.
The test `i <= 3` is now false (4 <= 3), so the loop ends. The body does not run again.
The program continues after the loop and prints 6.

code.title: for, while, for...of
code.caption: Add `20` to the array, then swap `break` for `continue` and compare the output.

walk.text: A `for` loop: start `i` at 0, test before each pass, add 1 after each pass.
`while` repeats until its test fails. Here the pass count depends on the data.
`for...of` hands you each value. `continue` skips 4; `break` stops the loop at 10.

pitfalls: Update the counter inside a `while` loop, or the test never fails and it runs forever.
Use `for...of` for array values; `for...in` gives keys as strings, such as '0'.
Write `i < prices.length`, not `<=`; `<=` reads one item past the end, giving `undefined`.

quiz.why: `i = 1` is skipped by `continue`. At `i = 3` the loop stops, so only 0 and 2 were added.

takeaway: Test, run, update, repeat. Pick the loop that matches what you know.

starters: When should I use while instead of for?
What happens if the test is false on the first pass?
How do I stop an infinite loop?
